Two words: Full Disclosure. If I'm going to read or watch a pre/review I want to know if this person is good at the game genre, bad at it, or doesn't normally even play games. If you tell me the truth long enough you'll have my trust enough for me to believe your scoring is accurate. When I see my friend posting rave reviews about a new Indie game, I'm inclined to believe him/her. If I'm not a fan of the genre, I still know that the game is a good addition to it because I have a level of trust with my friend and know that I'm not being pandered to. When I say, "Oh, I thought Mario Odyssey was just good" (My actual opinion, I'm sorry. I thought Sunshine was better) I expect people who know me to take my word as it is, while people who don't to take it with a grain of salt.

Should the person be good? Yes! Should they be the only people who get to write the review? I don't think so. But I want to know where they stand. I'm not a pro by any stretch of the imagination, but I'm proficient at all genres of game because I understand the mechanics that go into them. I admit that I suffer at RTS and MOBA, but I can still perform when I'm in a team and receiving instructions. It's simple enough once you've played enough of the genre, so if you're bad but need to get work done you'll just have to take the hit and write a few lopsided articles. Just be transparent and don't play the facade of excellence. When you treat your readers/viewers with respect they'll learn to trust you.

Okay, I actually have another theory pertaining to E. Gadd and Bowser Jr. Let me start off like this: 
Where did Bowser Jr. come from? Bowser has no wife. There's no Queen Koopa. And, the ending of Sunshine confirms that Peach is not Jr's mother. Nowhere in any Nintendo game is Bowser Jr. shown to have a mother. 
Now, search up "Baby Bowser." Baby Bowser is the grown up Bowser, just at Bowser Jr's age. Comparing the two, they look COMPLETELY IDENTICAL except for Jr's bib. What do we know now? That Bowser Jr. is physically identical to Bowser when he was a child. 

So, how does this work? Well, the easiest solution is obviously cloning. But Bowser is nowhere near the technological or intellectual level needed to clone himself. He also doesn't have the tools... You probably see where this is going. Well, E. Gadd DEFINITELY was in contact with Bowser at the time of Sunshine (Bowser Jr's origin). Since E. Gadd supplied Jr. with his paintbrush, is it really a stretch to say that he provided the tech to create him in the first place, using Bowser's DNA? Think about it. Bowser wants to defeat Mario in any way possible. A scientist coming up to him and offering to make him an heir (for a price) who would TOTALLY be able to kidnap Peach this time? Bowser would take that offer. This would also explain why E. Gadd just HANDED Bowser Jr. his paintbrush: he was arming his own little creation. This explains why Bowser might be awkward about his son asking who his mother was, and why he lied and said it was Peach. Now, there's no conclusive evidence, this is just the only theory I could come up with that had no obvious holes. Give it a thought.

Here are six tips to increase your chance of survival.

1. Kick your chair away, and stand up at all times, crouching down. Keep your right hand on the mouse to switch through cameras, and always keep your left arm extended out at all times, so that you always have an arm available. Taking even one, or two seconds to stand up to close the doors could mean life, or death.

2. Never check any other of the cameras except for the ones facing the doors. That way, you don’t waste any time not looking at the most important areas. Since there’s only one round of this game, and it only lasts for an hour, learning the animatronic’s patterns has greatly lost its value, especially since there are no do-overs.

3. Turn off your desk lamp, and use your flashlight. Since flashlights have batteries for several hours, and do not affect your power percentage, turning on your desk lamp is a crippling factor.

4. When a key camera (Either one facing the doors) goes offline, immediately shut the door the camera is supposed to be watching, so that you don’t have a blind spot.

5. If you find yourself panicking, shut down both doors for no more than 15 seconds, and calm yourself quickly when you know that you’re safe. In that last 5 seconds, thoroughly check the cameras to make sure that an animatronic didn’t sneak up behind one while you were calming yourself.

6. Take heavy breathers, and mentally prepare yourself before you go in, and memorize all of these factors. Reassure yourself constantly with quick, and easy to remember sentences whenever you feel anxiety. Make sure that these sentences are grounded in truth, and not meaningless to help your situation like, “It’ll be okay,” or “I’m fine.”

With Chapter 4 in mind, there are few things I’d like to theorize about the story as a whole and make predictions for chapter 5. Spoilers below. You have been warned.
I have something I’d like to point out about Henry. Based on the Chapter 4 resurrection screen and the fact that save points are Bendy statues, many people have begun theorizing that Henry us starting to be, or already is, corrupted by the ink. Now, there is one huge piece of evidence supporting this that nobody to my knowledge has pointed out. Evil Alice’s main fear is of being touched by one of the ink creatures, particularly Bendy, because she will be reverted back into a slug-like ink creature rather than a semi-humane ink angel. Now tell me, how do we first encounter Bendy? By getting close enough to the planks blocking the ink machine for Bendy to appear and swipe at us. My theory dear readers, is that Bendy manages to grab or touch Henry for a split-second, and in that moment he became corrupted by the ink. Now this will tie into my overall prediction for chapter 5, but I have one other topic I’d like to discuss; “Bendy,” aka the ink demon Bendy that has haunted us since Chapter 1.
Now, at this point we all pretty much know Bendy is Joey Drew. There is a small part of me that feels like The Meatly will pull a fast one on us and reveal Bendy to be someone else, it’s a highly unlikely scenario at this point in time, but I digress. In Chapter 4, Bendy takes a much more “passive” role towards us, not attacking us while we are in the vents and even defending us from The Projectionist. The question is, why? Every time he has appeared in previous chapters, Bendy has tried to kill us or attack us. Some people believe Bendy is toying with us. Others think it it is because Bendy isn’t as antagonistic as we first believed. The true answer, however, lies in the ideas of Joey Drew himself. His tape in chapter 4 reveals that Joey was far less pleasant than he seemed in the one from chapter 3, revealing the “belief can cheat death” motto was simply more of a marketing campaign rather than a true philosophy. Tapes from Susie reveal Joey was talking behind her back while trying to manipulate her to further his own goals. This all, at least to me, suggests Joey has a serious case of hubris. Now think about Bendy, who is all but confirmed to be Joey Drew, and the duality of his actions towards Henry. My belief is Joey is trying to play God, manipulating Henry in order to gain full control of the studio and eliminate his enemies. Think about it. While Bendy only appears to us after we turn on the ink machine in chapter 1, we KNOW Bendy had existed long before that moment, evidenced by Alice’s description of the hierarchy of the studio in chapter 3. So why would he wait until the ink machine is on to attack Henry? Simple. Bendy wants the ink machine on so he can have its power on his side, and use the ink it expels to further control the studio. Once the machine is on, Bendy attacks and sends Henry fleeing to the exit only to fall into the floor, weakened by large output of ink. Then in Chapter 2, Bendy takes the opportunity presented by Henry’s capture to eliminate Sammy. While this may seem counterproductive as Sammy worshipped Bendy like a God, it makes sense when you realize someone with a personality like Joey’s wouldn’t want ANYONE in position to threaten him. Now you may wondering, who could pose a threat to Bendy. Well, think about those he considers enemies. Sammy, The Projectionist, “Alice.” Bendy is threatened by the existence of other semi-human ink creatures. Now one may ask why those inky people, called “The Lost Ones,” aren’t included in this. My theory is that the Lost Ones are precursors to searchers, and as they continue to be exposed to the ink they will slowly decay into these mindless beasts. Now think back to the list of names I gave before. How was Bendy able to rid himself of each of those names? Henry. Henry’s capture caused Sammy to summon Bendy, allowing the ink demon to execute him. Henry hiding in the Miracle Station was what distracted The Projectionist long enough for Bendy  ti launch a surprise attack and decapitate him. While Bendy didn’t directly kill Alice, who was it that distracted Alice as she got stabbed in the stomach by Allison? Henry. Bendy is manipulating Henry towards his enemies, distracting them kong enough for Bendy to deliver an execution. So why does he attack in Chapter 3. Well, two reasons depending on the situation. His random attacks are likely incentives, trying ti get Henry to move faster, as he wants him to be in a situation that allows Bendy to eliminate Alice. When he attacks after the destruction of the Bendy cutouts, this is likely from a combination of being enraged by the cutouts removal and the resentment towards Alice for manipulating Henry, a right that only HE has (again this ties into the whole Hubris idea). To reiterate, Bendy is playing God of the studio, and Henry is his unknowing prophet.
Now for Chapter  predictions. Let’s start off with the after-credit image for Chapter 4, depicting the Lost Ones surrounding the dead body of Alice. My belief is that they are there on the orders of Bendy, their inky lord and savior, in order to corrupt her and drag her back into the inky abyss; the same fate she dreaded in Chapter 3. Bendy’s obvious motivation for this would be to punish Alice for antagonizing him for so long and even using his own pawn against him in Chapter 3. I have a feeling The Meatly will include a miniboss in Chapter 5 that resembles Alice to hint towards her fate. Maybe the achievement will be something like “Susie’s fate,” simultaneously confirming who the evil Alice was and what happened to her after Chapter 4. Now, combining the ideas in the previous two paragraphs, I think Chapter 5 will show Henry discovering his corruption and trying to resist the call giving into the ink hive mind. The main goal of Chapter 5 will likely be to shutdown the ink machine while Bendy attempts to stop you. Henry, with the help of Allison Angel and Tom Boris, will ultimately succeed and a boss fight against the ink God Bendy himself will commence. That’s where I’ll end because the rest of my ideas are mostly baseless headcanons that I don’t want to associate with truly evidenced ideas. And remember, that’s just a theory, a GAME Theory. Thanks for reading.

So, this was an interesting episode, but there are also a lot of problems with it. You're explaining Campbell being in the time paradox as a simulation, yet Campbell wasn't around at that time either. Sure he was in MGS Portable Ops, but his voice is that of an old man. AI system wasn't in place either, so that's hard to do. As for the CQC elements, every soldier Snake trains in the Big Boss saga knows it. It's hard to do, but being instructed by the dude who invented it has to help, hence the medic would know it as well. 

As for the historical innacuracies... Why would Zero, as meticulous ad he is, add a comment about the boss training in a fascility being made literally last year? He wouldn't be like "oh yes, that makes sense! I really want to let him know about that random place".

The inaccuracies don't stop there either. Look at the Les Enfants Terribles project. Liquid, with his blond hair and Solid with his Brown hair are being passed off as dominant and recessive gene clones. Which... Is also pretty inaccurate. Calorie mate was a brand deal. Virtuous mission vs. Virtual mission is probably just a little script choice as we had the same corny effect in Metal Gear Solid 2 with the "did you just say nerd?"-line Raiden spouts.

And mind you. Raiden, for all his VR training and all that... Was keenly aware it was VR. For him to undergo the transformation into becoming like Snake, he had to relive the same things pretty much, only in real time. If they couldn't hypnotically transform him into Solid Snake in 2005-ish, a dude who used to eat gunpowder to dull his senses... How'd Zero do it in 1983/84? Just because he was in a coma? They could've put Raiden in a coma too.

All in all... Fantastic episode. I know these aren't to be the one true theory or whatever, but more a way to make you think outside the box, and that made it really interesting. For me personally, I wouldn't say it's very plausible, but the episode is really good none the less. Thanks!

There's actually only one explanation that accounts for every clue in BotW - including the things this video missed, like how the Great Deku Tree isn't found in any of the Fallen Hero Timeline, or Gorons, for that matter, plus things like the references to Twilight or sailing across the sea, and would also take into account the DLC items and Amiibos:

What if BotW is the next tie-together game?

After the timeline is split for so long, BotW is the point where they converge again.  This is explained in-game through the fact that they worship the Great Goddess Hylia, instead of Din, Farore, and Nayru (which hasn't been mentioned in any other game but Skyward Sword).  This would also explain why the Triforce doesn't seem to exist in BotW.  The timelines all lead to BoW, no matter how OoT played out.

Things the video failed to account for:
- The Great Deku Tree isn't in any Fallen Hero games, but it is in BotW.
- Same with the Goron race.  While Zoras, Rito, and Koroks can be explained, there is no Goron counterpart in the Fallen Hero timeline.  The Rito is a bit of a stretch, too.
- Same for the Gerudos.  Link Between Worlds has a gang of thieves in Lorule, but not in Hyrule.  Canon says that Ganon wiped out the Gerudos when he won since they turned against him in OoT.
- The Mirror of Twilight can be found in BotW (the Fragmented Monument).
- The Provinces of Hyrule are first introduced in Twilight Princess (Faron, Eldin, and Lanayru)
- The Arbiter's Grounds from TP is in BotW.
- Crenel Hills from the Minish Cap is in BotW.
- Goponga Island, Kanalet Ridge, Mabe Village Ruins, Martha's Landing, Tal Tal Peak, Tabhal Woods, Ukuku Plains, and Koholit Rock from Link's Awakening are in BotW.
- Horon Lagoon is the same name as Horon Town in Oracle of Seasons
- Linebeck Island in BotW is named for the captain in Phantom Hourglass.
- Lulu Lake, Mikau Lake, Toto Lake were named for the band in Majora's Mask.
- Mount Daphnes in BotW was name for King Daphnes (King of Red Lions) from Windwaker.
- Ralis Pond was named for Prince Ralis of the Zoras from TP.
- The Divine Beasts were named for heroes of the different races: Vah Nabooris (Nabooru, OoT), Vah Rudania (Darunia, OoT), Vah Ruta (Ruto, OoT), and Vah Medoh (Medli, Windwaker).
- The Tingel, Ankel, Knuckel, and Davdi Islands are all named for the four residents of Tingle Tower in Wind Waker - Tingle, Ankle, Knuckle, and David Jr.
- The flowers around the Master Sword pedestal in BotW align with the flowers around the pedestal in Link to the Past
- and much more.

You might dismiss a few of these as trivia, but there's just as much evidence for Adult and Child timelines as there is for Fallen Hero.  Nintendo officially stated that BotW takes place in the Adult Link timeline, but taking all evidence into account points to all three timelines converging here.

Actually, there could be a name for that number if you wanted. The way to name number places after million in english is to just count in latin then add illion at the end. So billion (2/bi), trillion (3/tria), quadrillion (4/quattuor). So if you look at these number places, each one is effectively adding 3 to the power a 10 is multiplied to. 1 billion is 10^9, 1 trillion is 10^12, and 1 quadrillion is 10^15. So to find the equivalent latin number for that number we need to divide it by three, then subtract by 1, because the first three powers of ten aren't in latin yet. So 12,431/3=4,143.66. Subtract 1 and we have 4,142.66. This means the number place is going to be one hundred, of the Latin word for 4,137. This would be quattuor milia, centum quadraginta duo. So applying this to number places, we have quattuormiliacentumquadragintabillion. 
So, our final name is one hundred and eighty quattuormiliacentumquadragintabillion. (this is assuming you wanted to keep that 1.8 in the number. You didn't include it at the end, but I feel like it should be included)

We all know that Bulbasaur wasn't in this because it would be the obvious winner

 First off, Hyper Beam is not the most powerful move in the first generation. Sure, it has the highest base power, but the user has to wait a turn after using it. Bulbasaur can learn the true most powerful moves in the first generation: Leech Seed and Sleep Powder. Leech Seed deals fixed damage to your opponent every turn (regardless of type except Grass) and then heals your Bulbasaur the same amount. Sleep Powder had pretty much 100% accuracy and, unlike in later Pokemon games, it took your Pokemon the entire turn to wake up. This means that if Bulbasaur is faster than your opponent, they don’t get to move at all.
 To counteract Charizard’s high special stat, Venusaur learns the move growth, which will power up Venusaur’s Razor Leaf attack and its Special Defense at the same time (in the first generation) making Charizard’s special attacks deal less damage. In later games, Bulbasaur can learn Synthesis and Giga Drain, healing more than Charmander can deal out. Thanks to Bulbasaur’s Poison type, it doesn’t have to worry about being poisoned, which is an excellent ability for a tank Pokemon. It also gives it access to the Black Sludge, which allows you to give the Leftovers to another member of your team. When Venusaur mega evolves, its ability Thick Fat reduces Charizard’s STAB attacks. All the while, Leech Seed is sapping away more health from your opponent.
 Although Charizard learns more HM’s than Venusaur, that doesn’t make it better. That just makes it more “useful” OUTSIDE of battle. Even though it’s not the winner of the popularity contest, it doesn’t mean that Bulbasaur isn’t the best Pokemon.

I don't want to sound like a know-it-all or anything, but I sort of figured that the system that YouTube uses for recommendations wasn't completely in the hands of the company, because I'm very aware of how fast and popular YouTube has grown over the years. It's really great to have someone explain how it works in a way most older demographics would understand. Even as a middle school student, I found it fascinating, so thank you for that. Secondly, the way that YouTube is evolving seems like it would be terrifying to much smaller, lesser known channels. I really hope that as the site grows, channels won't change their content to become more well-known. I know the point of this video was to help other growing channels and educate them to be smarter with the choices they make with their videos, but I hope it doesn't necessarily change their original identities. I personally enjoy smaller channels just as much as people like Markiplier and Pewdiepie (well, I don't really Pewdiepie that much, but just as an example.) I like diversity, and it's an important factor in YouTube's growth. I just hope that channels focus on the love and care they put in each of their videos, not the likes or subscribers that they receive because them. Lastly, I don't think I'll ever do much with my YouTube channel. I have one stupid video that has to do with Undertale, and I know most people consider it "dead." But I do think that this video is helpful for people who are trying to become more well known. Though I personally will never really do much on YouTube, it's nice to know some channels are willing to help other channels grow and flourish. So thank you for demonstrating that.

At one point, the Mushroom Kingdom was hosting a party & Mario’s parents brought along the two twins, leaving them to be babysat by Toadsworth. From there, he goes on a huge adventure with his future self & saving Baby Peach. As a baby, he gets inspired by the red & green heroes, so becomes more heroic in his actions & motives. WAIT! This theory has a huge hole in it! You yourself have said that the lead creator of the game said that unkindled ones are people who tried to link the flame in the past but failed and were burn to ashes. However, the first cinematic of Dark Souls 3 gives us an extra clue, showing that it is the Soul of Cinder that does the burning, which means that, in order to become an unkindled one, you have to have reached the Kiln of the First Flame but failed to defeat the Soul of Cinder.
That makes it impossible for the playable character of DS3 to be anyone who used to serve the kingdom in recent years, and in a way precludes the other unkindled ones from being people who have lived in the current cycle.
Prince Lothric was supposed to be the one to link the flame in the DS3 cycle, but he refused, so the three Lords of Cinder before him (probably) were brought back to do it in his place, but they refused as well. Only then unkindled were brought back. This sequence of events makes it impossible for any other warrior to have tried to link the flame this cycle. Dark Souls 3 has introduced this more or less new concept that you need to have something specific in order to link the flame. In DS1 you needed the Lord souls to appease the Lordvessel; in DS2 you needed the four primale bonfires to be lit in order to enter the castle and the four great souls in order to be eligible to taking the throne. Now in DS3 you need all five embers in order to open the path to the Kiln of the First Flame.  Which is why the unkindled one needs to kill the lords of cinder. He couldn't just go and try to beat the Soul of Cinder, he needed the souls and embers of the Lords of Cinder to go there.

TL:DR: There is no way the Ashen one we play as can be anyone from the current cycle, as no one has tried to link the fire yet, as it was prince Lothric's duty.

Another thing is you can start as the Assassin class. The Assassin armor is VERY similar to the Black Hand set. The Assassin also starts as the highest level and very strong equipment. This makes sense because most beginners would probably choose this class as it gives them the best opportunity to succeed. Also, the class has a very high Dex stat which is what the Hunter ring provides, so it only makes sense. Interesting theory, except there's one NPC you've forgotten about. One that could be seen as opposed to Lothric and Lorian. A Scholar, not unlike the ones who tutored the young Prince, who was perhaps sent to make amends for the mistakes of his peers by helping you subdue the final Lord; Orbeck of Vinheim. 

All of Lothric's family are steeped in Sorcery; Oceiros is attempting to follow in Seath's footsteps, the Grand Archives are geographically located atop the old Duke's Archives and Lothric himself uses a unique form of Faith-based Crystal magic. He shares a physical resemblance to Priscilla, Seath's crossbreed daughter with Gwynevere from the first game, who also represents a melding of Faith and Sorcery. 

What you first meet Orbeck, he has set up a makeshift study in the swamp, and immediately after finding him, you encounter the Crystal Sage boss, an enemy later found in the Grand Archives. The Crystal Sage seems pretty out of place in the swamp, unless it was attempting to track down and stop Orbeck at the behest of the other Scholars. When you meet Orbeck at Firelink Shrine, he says; "No matter the victim's stature, every killing has a consequence..." He specifically mentions that the victim's status doesn't matter, whether it's a commoner or even a member of the Royal Family. 

He also confesses to being more of an Assassin than a Sorcerer. His armour, the Clandestine Coat, states; "These were covert agents who excelled at manipulating sound", maybe hinting that Orbeck's aural Sorcery and training as an Assassin makes him a prime candidate to kill the largely handicapped Royal Family of Lothric; Oceiros is blind, Lorian is lame and Lothric is frail, and all of them have their eyes obscured in some way, meaning they would most likely rely on sound, something Orbeck can use to his advantage. It's also interesting that the only fight you can summon him for is Lothric and Lorian. 

Further, Yuria of Londor, who wants the Fire to fade, tells you to kill Orbeck, perhaps because it was Orbeck's task to subdue the Prince, just like it was Anri, Siegward and Hawkwood's task to topple their respective Lords. She goads you by telling you he threatens your position as Lord of Hollows. If you trust Yuria and kill Orbeck, that's perhaps one less person to persuade you to link the Fire, allowing Yuria's, and by extension the Lords of Cinder's, plans to come to fruition instead.

After a scanthrough of the lore of the dark souls universe (Vaati videos), I have concluded that the identity of the ashen one does not matter. In fact I would argue that the identity of the ashen one is deliberately left anonymous by Fromsoft to enhance the immersive atmosphere of Dark Souls.

Take into account the description of the starting classes you choose at the start of dark souls 3. 

The Knight reads: "An obscure knight of poor renown who collapsed roaming the land. Sturdy, owing to high vitality and stout armor." - Source: Fextralife wiki (since I didn't pay attention to the class descriptions when I chose my class and instead looked for best armour).

Aside from this all other information that directly links with the player character is in the descriptions of the starting gifts, and they are even more vague than the misc. items you discover throughout the game (Worker's trousers has more lore than these).

Hell, even the NPCs of the souls games belittles the player character, take into account Eygon of Carim. When you first meet him he is not even remotely courteous to you, instead saying things like: "All you faceless Undead, behaving as if you deserve respect."

By giving us little lore about our own characters and giving so many hints and references to the bosses we slay and the npcs we meet increases the opressive atmosphere of the game and raises the presence of the bosses. That is unlike games such as WoW, your character is no hero, and no chosen one. Rather than being told you are great you start as the bottom feeders of the barrel that is the souls universe, and you claw your way up and when you finally beat the challenges the game throws at you, it just feels that much sweeter.

I wonder how the postscarcity situation plays into that.

You see, in the Fallout universe the world's population is much smaller than it was in the past, yet the land is littered with scrap, food, weapons and ammunition meant for a much larger population. You can play through all of Fallout 4 in survival mode (where you have needs like hunger and thirst) living entirely off all the preserved prewar food you find everywhere. And in any 'modern' Fallout game you play, by the end of the game you'll have stacks and stacks and stacks of weapons, armors, clothes and ammunition. You don't need to buy anything.

What this means is that people don't really need to produce anything. You want a house? Plenty of those around. You want electronics? Take as many as you can carry. You want food? Don't bother starting up a farm, there's free food all over the place. So what incentive is there for people to live constructive, productive lives? There's very little value in anything they could make. The only things that are really valuable are weapons and armor, and most of those are prewar as well. Because there's no real gain to be had in being productive, 80-90% of humans you find in the Commonwealth and the Capital Wasteland are raiders. They get doped up and fight over piles of junk because that's all there is left to do for them.

The radiation from the bombs would have dissipated a LONG time before these games started. The background radiation in the Fallout series is largely concentrated in, relatively small pockets throughout the wasteland from leaking barrels of reactor waste, spent fuel, or damaged small scale reactors( that would have powered, well, damn near everything in this universe) melting down. And with many inhabitants having had access to, or having recovered, prewar technology, it stands to realize that that they could avoid the many of the more concentrated pockets of radiation. This is especially true of those that came from the vaults, as the vault dweller's Pip-Boys have inbuilt Geiger counters, they likely also have access to stores of anti-radiation drugs such as Rad-X and Radaway, and quite possibly radiation suits. Even some tribal societies of the wasteland have created homegrown anti-radiation drugs. And don't even get me started on the G.E.C.K.

The creation/machine that Gaster fell into is not a Determination injection machine, but a DT *Extraction* machine. It removes determination. 

Now, when monsters are injected with determination, they fuse with more matter/dust/monsters, and start to melt. Naturally, extraction of Determination could split a monster soul/body/mind. Thus you'd get two* monsters and the original husk, split on personality and ability. sans having greater power, Papyrus being, as Undyne put it, "pretty freaking tough."

Now, as for the Husk and journal entry, I'd imagine what was left of the original Gaster, effectively empty of determination, tried to quickly fix himself by injecting determination. He recovers temporarily (as did Alphys's test subjects), and made the final entry while talking to Papyrus and sans. Then he began to melt. Who knows what sans and Papyrus did afterwards - trying to "go back" or "fix Gaster"...but ultimately, Gaster became a melted memory.

Now, Memory is a good choice of words, as there is one other monster tied to Gaster: Memoryhead. Memoryhead is an amalgamate, but the only one to not resemble any known monster. It has a faint resemblance to a Gaster Blaster fused with a brain. It's bullet attacks summon smiling white faces (Gasters?). It has no physical substance - it talks through your phone and gains health by absorbing your attack. Also, a phrase it says is "Lorem ipsum docet", while a filler phrase in code, translates to "Pain teaches."

Vikings used bows quite often in combat, as well as spears and javelins. The average soldier was expected to carry a bow and spear when called to war. The neighbor is not a "bad guy".

Let's go back to the gameplay section where you access the basement:
MatPat described the sign saying "Hide Here" as a laughably simplistic trap, but what if it wasn't?  What if it was there to immediately inform people where to hide if something bad were to happen?  When you go down to the basement you hear a woman shout "RUN!", see shuffling shadows, and the room is empty.  Soon after the neighbor himself enters the basement and then enters the "hide here" room and shuts the door behind him "long enough for the player to escape".

Now if we assume the neighbor is a good guy and the "hide" room is essentially a 'backup panic room' then the neighbor would enter it after hearing "RUN!" for two reasons:
1.  He wants to make sure the woman and child are ok. (goes in to check on them)
2.  He hides in the room for his own safety.

Since there are two beds, one mattress and one crib, combined with the fact that you hear a woman's voice and a baby's, suggests #2 is correct.  The woman was not shouting "RUN!" to inform her babbling baby or herself, but rather the neighbor (she mistook you for a more dangerous invader).  The reason why the neighbor is constantly barricading and booby-trapping his house, the reason why his basement is a fortified safe-room with an additional safe-room inside of it, is because himself, his wife, and his child, are being hunted by something.  If we assume devil-magic is actually involved it wouldn't be hard to imagine that one of them made a deal with the devil and now said devil wants his "pound of flesh".

They're being hunted and while the wife and child hide in the safe room the father takes the risk of being out in the open in order to better protect his family.  A deal with the devil might also explain how he can afford to make these ridiculous additions to his house and get away with it (suburban neighborhood associations can be rather strict).  It's also possible he can afford to stay out in the open because the hunter-demon is more interested in the wife and/or child rather than the father.

Also, in order for this theory to work the hunter-demon would have to be the type that has to enter a premises manually rather than just teleporting into the family room.

I have some speculation on the setting of this game, but first, a few questions.

Why does the neighbor only drop you outside of your house when you've been poking around? Why doesn't he call the police? They don't have any evidence and can't legally search, but they may very well get it if you continue snooping. Why doesn't he kill you until you open the exit in one of the Alphas? Speaking of the exit, there are a zillion other exits in that house, why does only _that_ one have a sign? Why is that one so special? What's on the other side of that wall? And why does it seem to lead to different places between Alphas?

Why does he bury you in the yard _alive_? In his backyard with a grave marker. Seem a strange and risky way to quickly dispose of someone who is causing you trouble. He'd have to have had the grave already dug, and a coffin already on hand! Wouldn't someone have noticed?

You are already dead. Likely in Limbo, struggling to redeem yourself or just trying to pass through to where you're "supposed" to be.

1: The Etecoons and Dachoras has strong identifiable lifesigns, something all X-Parasites coppies lack.

The reason that claiming copyright over an entire genre is especially concerning, is because it removes competition. Without competition, the developers don't feel a need to invest as much money and effort into the game, resulting in a noticeable drop in quality. A drop in quality could be the start of a decline the video game industry, possibly leading into another video game crash. One example of this is in EA's Madden games. NFL2k was considered by many to be a superior game to Madden, and as such EA made an exclusivity deal with the NFL to make sure that only they can create NFL football video games. We now have low-quality yearly releases of Madden, because EA has no competition to fear. With developers claiming copyright over an entire genre, we would see this effect in all of gaming.

The funny thing is, these decisions to copyright claim stuff are not even made by game creators themselves. Nintendo has taken down several fan games, but Shigeru Miyamoto himself has stated his opinion being that "fan games shouldn't be taken down". Something similar happened with a MLP fan game, where Hasbro took it down, but Lauren Faust, the newest show's creator, disapproved of it and even personally helped with a replacement fan game for it afterwards.

So yes, games like Undertale and FNaF being indie games is actually a VERY important factor because, for such games, the brand's creator is also the brand's owner and has full power over it, but that is not the case for big brands like Nintendo or Hasbro, where game creators eventually lose the power to decide what to do with their brand since it is technically no longer theirs, even though they created it. Unfortunately, these things will keep happening as long as brands are owned by companies with monetary interests instead of creators who love and care about their product.

This video claims that Phoenix stole the wiretap that was in April May's hotel room, but that is not the case. If you look carefully, the wiretap is "added to the court record". If he had physically taken the evidence with him, it would say something like "slipped into pocket", words that are used later on in the series. Point 2: the receipt

This video also claims that Phoenix nonchalantly collected evidence after Mia Fey's murder in the second case instead of calling the police, but that claim is bogus when you look at the sequence of events at that part of the game. This is what happened:

Phoenix, being the second person to arrive at the scene, finds his mentor dead and her sister, Maya, in tears. She passes out and Phoenix places her in a sofa in the next room. He then does the sensible thing and checks if Mia is dead. For all he knew, she could have been unconscious. Her body goes cold after he puts his hand on her shoulder, so he concludes that she is, in fact, dead. He then looks at the scene, taking note of the Thinker, the broken glass light stand and the receipt with the word "Maya" on in blood. (The phrase "added to court record" is used.) He then tries to call the police but the phone in the office was tampered with, so he is unable to. He then finds Maya awake and, after learning of her name, tells her about the note. The police arrive at the scene. Detective Gumshoe finds the note next to the body and arrests Maya after also learning about her name and concluding that Mia wrote her killer's name on the receipt. 

When did Phoenix conceal any evidence here? He didn't! If he did, Detective Gumshoe wouldn't have found the note in the first place, and thus wouldn't have suspected Maya when he did. Plus, the evidence that Phoenix found was still there for the police to find later, which is how both Detective Gumshoe and Prosecutor Edgeworth knew about it in the trial.

The way I see it, if you're able to really get into Max's head as a character, it's extremely unlikely she'd make the choice to sacrifice Chloe in that moment. Forget what the 'right' or 'wrong' choice is. From a utilitarian perspective, sacrificing Chloe will save more lives. But Max isn't an impassive hero. She's an 18-year-old girl, that was just drugged and assaulted by a maniac after watching her best friend get shot in the head. She's allowed to be weak, allowed to be selfish. Max, by that point in the story, is an emotional wreck. It's easy to say the Sacrifice Chloe ending is better as a player, in your room, under no psychological duress. But your average person is absolutely not going to give up the only good thing presently in their life under that much stress, consequences be damned. I'm not saying Sacrifice Chloe is an invalid ending. Choose what you want. I just think that it wouldn't be Max's choice, which is why I went Bae Over Bay.

Also, worth mentioning that Chloe's dialogue when she's asking you to sacrifice her is very specific. I think it's less meant to demonstrate that Chloe wants to die so much as it is demonstrating that she's grown out of her selfishness (to some extent). Even in that situation, she still stipulates to Max that "no matter what you choose, I know you'll make the right choice." That doesn't sound to me like someone that would be inexplicably bitter about still being alive. Yeah, survivor's guilt is a thing. But the short truck scene we get in the Sacrifice Arcadia Bay ending depicts pretty clearly that, at least for the time, Max and Chloe are on good terms. And if you believe Word of God, they're "definitely in a relationship".

Okay, at the risk of being *that guy*, here's something I noticed that would throw off your numbers.

You analogized her legs to a rock on a string. That's considered a point mass. Basically, the formula you used assumes all the mass is in her foot. A leg is considered a rigid body (inb4 [generic NSFW joke]), which means you need to take into account their moment of inertia, or the fact that the mass of her legs is distributed across the entire length, unlike a rock on a string, where all the mass is at the end. The formula for this is (moment of inertia)*(rotational speed)^2.

Remember that the energy sword only loses ten percent of its charge on the killing blow. You can strike an enemy repeatedly with no loss of charge, and it's only the final strike which actually kills the opponent when the sword's battery depletes. And even then, there are exceptions. The energy sword expels not ten percent but rather two to three percent of its charge every time it lands a killing blow against a Flood, because the Flood are heavily decomposed and putrefied, so their bodies are much easier to cut through and therefore require less battery from the sword.

I really don’t know what it is with some people;

For me, that ending poem for Minecraft, in a strange way, is one of the best things I’ve ever read. 

In fact, I’m inclined to believe that that conversation/poem has roots in existentialism and that all it may really be saying is that, given how smart we humans are and how much smarter we will inevitably become in the future, whether or not we realize it, we are all more powerful than we know. 

In general, we humans are lucky enough to have been made of just the right elements and ingredients to be able to exist at all; however, on top of that, we have the amazing abilities of being able to utilize our surroundings and create...

To be able to care about things at all... 

To be able to love things...

To be able to recognize that we exist within a universe...

Also, think about it:

Billions and billions of years ago, we humans didn’t exist... and now we’re here - not just as human beings, but as beings that spawned from the universe itself...

Beings that just so happen to inhabit this planet, continuously advancing as a species that is bound to end up leaving and expanding beyond Earth, and, at some point, actively utilize and create with whatever else the universe has to offer, such as other planets and even the stars themselves.

Lastly, along with the poem mentioning how life is a “long dream” and Minecraft is a “short dream”... just like the theory explains in this video, I really would like to think that that’s implying that playing video games, in general, is not really a waste of time and that they can be a valid alternative for us to try and understand our place in this world, or even this universe, from very different perspectives.

So, you could say that that conversation that serves as the “ending” for Minecraft provides some much needed perspective and context for a game that, basically, has you playing a simplified version of real life, if you exclude the fictional monsters.

Overall, I really wish many other people would realize that there truly is even a little bit of meaning to this game we call “Minecraft”; 

That, essentially, it’s part of our human nature to create... To bring things into existence via utilizing nature itself.

Because we can. 

Because, in a strange way, it’s almost as if the universe made us this way on purpose...

Anyway, I enjoyed this video - very thought-provoking. :)

In fact, it’s so thought-provoking that I very much believe most of what’s said in this video are factual statements about this near-philosophical “ending” to Minecraft. 

To me, it’s not just a theory;

I don’t think there’s currently any other video on YouTube that could have explained this ending any better.

Similar to how many chibi-style games like Harvest Moon, have basically every single item greatly enlarged when held by the player character. This isn't to show that, for example, a carrot is twice the size of your body and you can somehow magically eat it a bunch of them, but its actually just the game artists means of depicting a carrot in your hand, if they made it life-size then you would be holding a 2 pixel orange thing, but by greatly exaggerating its size of the carrot, the player can figure out what they are looking at easily. I'm sure its a similar principle with the rupee's, if they made them actual-size, no one would be able to find them, especially in the earlier games. With the lore that’s been released since this episode aired, I think we might be able to take this theory one step further. The Light and Dark might actually use the same energies, but for different purposes. Eris, in one of her cards, describes finding an Throne World made for the Light. Not made *of* the Light, but *for* the Light. Why would that exist? The Throne Worlds are created by the Hive’s magic, fueled by Dark energies, so how and/or why would the Light have one? 

To push from the Hive’s magic tangling with the Light, I’d like to propose my own theory. I think that the Guardians and the Hive both follow the Sword Logic, and we just don’t know it. Let’s take a look at how the Sword Logic works. Killing under the Sword Logic establishes your dominance over whatever you killed, and proves its unworthiness to exist in the “final universe”. The Hive also grow more powerful from killing, since killing feeds their worm symbiotes within them. The Guardians use this in almost the exact same way. We kill relentlessly, establishing our place in the universe over them, and we grow in power from killing them. How? Well, it’s no wonder the most powerful loot comes from killing the most powerful enemies. Atheon, Crota, Skolas, Oryx, Aksis, Calus (as a robot but whatever), Argos, Val Ca’Our, Riven, and Insurrection Prime all count as very, very powerful, since they’ve all killed many things for themselves. Strike bosses give strong loot as well, but not as strong, since they haven’t killed as much as their raid boss counterparts. When we kill them and equip that loot, it’s no wonder our “Light” level increases. Our Light is fueled by the same powers as the Dark, just used for a different purpose. 

So what do you all think? Is it a nonsense theory, or could this play into Destiny 3’s plot with Darkness abilities (at least, the one we think is going to exist)?

In my opinion Super Mario Odyssey makes this theory even stronger. It has Bowser kidnapping Peach just to marry her. He goes through a lot of trouble to make the wedding perfect too. He gets food, flowers, a ring, etc.

One last thing I thought I'd point out, in the modern Paper Mario games, Bowser doesn't seem to be on bad terms with Mario. In Sticker Star (I'm sorry but it still exists like it or not) and Color Splash, Bowser wasn't fully in control of himself, as evidenced after the battle against him in Color Splash, where he asks Mario if he just came to remind him if there was a kart race.

In the Origami King, Bowser and his minions don't seem to have any aggression to Mario. At all. In fact, Bowser serves as quite a major character, but more like the comedic side character if anything.

Now, why is this? Well, if you remember the beginning of Super Paper Mario, Count Bleck hosts a wedding between Bowser and Peach. Peach is forced into marrying Bowser. It's pretty clear that over the rest of the game, Bowser thinks he's actually married to Peach, much to Peach's dismay. Now that he got exactly what he wanted, he doesn't seem to be interested in world domination or anything after that. He seems to be on much better terms with Mario after the events of that game.

You might end up wondering, "But Bowser isn't on good terms with Mario in non-Paper Mario games!" Well, as established in Mario and Luigi: Paper Jam, the paper world and main world are two different universes.

Also, Paper Bowser and Bowser teaming up? It's possible the timeline for Paper Jam could have happened before Super Paper Mario. The game doesn't specify what exactly the Paper Mario characters were doing before being pulled from that book.

I think the LttP closing argument is entirely flawed. It's entirely based on the assumption that the original Zelda title is the ultimate game, and what all future games should be based on.

The truth of the matter is game design is an iterative process, and games evolve over time. You can't argue that OoT doesn't follow "Zelda standards" when really there are only 2-3 titles that follow that old standard. At this point there are many more games in the 3d vein, and have all tried there own respective variations on the franchise. 

Both games are phenomenal for their own reasons, and both inspire that feeling of adventure and exploration (personally, OoT did this MUCH better for me). For me, the win goes to OoT without question. I think Link Between Worlds showed that Zelda games on a 2d plane can be somewhat limited in their design, and opening up the world to the 3rd dimension added so much (and was done so well) that it cannot be denied. 

Also, judging by Miyamoto's description, he would've wanted as much immersion, exploration, and sense of adventure as possible. I think OoT does all of those things much better, and possibly with less effort.

Great video, but there was one thing I was wondering... You calculated about how much Fallout Caps would be worth in 1961, and then in 2015. However, the Fallout universe economy would continue until 2077, when the Great War happened and prices stopped changing. Due to inflation having a massive effect on the world considering all natural resources being used up, I wondered what caps would be worth in 2077. So I took it upon myself to figure it out. 

In order to figure out the value of caps I first figured out the value of gold in 2077. In order to do this, I had to figure out the % increase of another commodity. In Fallout 4, if you go to a Red Rocket station, the sign will say that ¨Class C Coolant¨ is $113.99 per gallon. Class A is cut off, but I´ll assume Class C is more of an average than Class A. I will also assume that ¨coolant¨ is effectively the same price as conventional gasoline would be and compare it as such. Comparing the gas prices of 1961 (~$0.27 per gallon) to the coolant  prices of 2077 gives a percent increase of 42,122% Now, multiplying the price of gold in 1961, being $35.50 per Troy ounce, by this 42,122% means that gold in 2077 would be worth $1,495,331 PER TROY OUNCE. HOLY CRAP. This would mean a 35 pound, 510 Troy ounce brick of gold would be worth $762,618,810. Finally, this means that a single Fallout bottlecap would be worth $71,206

Some comments to a lot of the big questions on the new Five Nights at Freddy's video. Hope they help clarify this a bit!

- "X Days before the party": This text before each minigame DOESN'T mean the nights featured in the game are all happening before bite shown in the Night 5 minigame. That's only true IF you're assuming time is linear and that each minigame takes place between each night, which is incredibly unlikely. As we've seen in past games, the minigames between nights are UNSTUCK in time, most often FLASHBACKS to events that happened. The pills, IV, and flowers support this assumption that a medical emergency (like the bite) already happened.

- The 1983 date on the TV, yes I was aware of it when writing the episode. That will be more fully addressed in the lore video!

- Phone Guy's comment about "surviving without a frontal lobe": Just because the kid goes limp in the mouth of Fredbear DOESN'T mean he died in that moment. It's highly likely he went into shock, blacked out, etc, from the injury, and was then rushed to the hospital. And the flatline in night 6, yes, it's likely that means the child died in those moments, BUT he still "lived" for a period of time before that -- the time between the bite and his eventual passing. So Phone Guy's comment isn't invalid -- he never specified HOW LONG the bite victim lived or that the victim was still alive, just that there was a period of time where the victim survived without a chunk of brain, which he found surprising.

MatPat. As a long time viewer and subscriber I applaud you for this video. Of course, the fact that all of you game (and film!) theorists have been working overtime lately to pump out more regular videos for us is worth applause enough. Think about it, traditional sports, card, and board games (such as baseball, poker, and scrabble) have been a part of American culture for ages. We just now are really beginning to get full families to gather around and play a freaking video game together. In nerd speak, video games aren't in the average American's cultural canon. 

What I'm getting at here is that I may have to wait another decade or two before I can watch the SC2 finals on the television. This is just because of the amount of time it will take for video gaming to further integrate with our society's norms. I find it humorous how many people are trying to justify their "Gaming ain't a sport!" by claim by saying there's no physical precision or not enough movement, then find no fault in games like Poker, Chess, Cup Stacking, Horse Racing, et al. being sports.  

Listen up: We're not saying that ALL gaming is a sport.  My playing football, soccer, and baseball with my son and the neighbors doesn't make me an athlete. It doesn't even make it a sport.  It's just a game as it's done for the fun of it without any serious competitive consideration, even as we follow the rules.  However, those players who build custom components to get the weights perfect for their hands?  The ones who practice with their team for hours on end and then watch their competitors' game videos to anticipate strategies?  The ones who've developed PRECISE MUSCLE MOVEMENTS to fulfill their needs in their chosen game?  The ones who take the time to learn exactly what each piece in the game can do in an otherwise balanced and fair playing field, making only the players' skill and ability to perform the difference between victory and defeat?  (EDIT: Adding the following line as I thought I'd included it)  The ones who take the time and energy to ensure that they meet all requirements to fit into a specific competitive organization's requirements so that they can actively participate in the advertised local, regional, national, and international competitions? (/EDIT) That's physical prowess, skill, and competition.  That's dedication and drive.  That, my friends, is when it becomes a sport.  It doesn't take away from your chosen preferred sports any more than the sports that are currently recognized by the older generation did for other sports. It's just simply a newer, different kind of sport.

I am a gamer.  I don't consider my personal gaming to be a sport and I'm okay with that.  I play to have fun and I don't rightly care if I come out on top in every single game as long as it was a fair game that was entertaining.  But those teams of players who dedicate that time, energy, devotion to winning their game with their team in an organized and regulated format?  They're playing their game as a sport.  It's no different than any other sport out there.  Just like any other sport, it has its tools and equipment.  And unless you can come up with an argument other than, "It's not physical enough," or the grossly tired, "The definition (that I won't link to) says...," then you're only arguing against it because it's *different.*

I find this entire debate to be fundamentally flawed by the question itself. The question of which game is more "artistic" is like asking whether a Labrador or a Golden Retriever is more dog! Art doesn't come in levels. Sure, the quality of art could be disputed. But comparing Pac-Man's abstract 8-bit ghost maze of pleasing colors and sounds to The Last of Us's realistic renderings and interesting story is even farther removed than comparing apples to oranges. It's comparing apples to fine china. The two games use completely different styles, have different goals, reasons for exists, historical context, and so on!
Certainly anyone can have an opinion on which game they like more and reasons why. But to say that one isn't art or is less like art than another doesn't even make sense.

(I'm posting this before watching the video) This is like asking which is more artistic between the Mona Lisa and Beethoven's music, or Salvador Dali's Un chien Andalou. They are all art, they all use forms that captivate us in different ways and express feelings, emotions, etc. I couldn't say which is 'more' artistic since I don't think something can be more artistic than something else. I can say which one I prefer, which one is better (in my opinion) but I can't make one less of an art form than another. The same goes to video-games. I definitely do believe that games are art forms and have always been.

In terms of overall quality, style, narrative, and mechanics, "The Last of Us" is the clear winner.

But a more nuanced look would have to take into account the times that each game was created.  Before PacMan, video games lacked much of an identity within the art world.  Many of the mechanics that we take for granted in modern games didn't exist at that time, making PacMan a pioneer into a new realm altogether.  The artistic leaps and bounds made in PacMan easily rival if not outright surpass the achievements made in "The Last of Us".

It is similar to comparing cave hieroglyphics to an image made in Photoshop.  One is clearly more advanced but it can be argued that the hierogyphics were more original and therefore more artistic.

The Rusted Iron Ring is certainly *helpful* in Blighttown and that water area in Darkroot Basin with the Hydra, but you can easily beat the game without the ring.

Also... Technically, the DS1 does tell you (albeit indirectly) where to go, since, unless you're really good at the game or managed to get a blunt weapon or divine weapon, the skeletons in the graveyard leading to the catacombs will eat you for lunch because you're not meant to go down there until you meet the requirements to survive down there. It's the reason that if you go the road leading to the Undead Burg, you only have, like... Four or five super easy hollow enemies to contend with.

It's the same as triggering that wyvern's appearance at the High Wall of Lothric in Dark Souls 3. You don't have to go up there unless you want the loot up there and it's a shortcut leading to a spot that you were going to go to anyway.


At the end of the day... I like to think of Dark Souls as being like the Mr. Miyagi of video games.

Matpat, you may understand anatomy, but this is the realm of fluid dynamics. This is the ratio of blood in the system vs space for that blood away from vital organs. You are correct that the body would not stand a whole human's worth of blood while legless, but look instead at the pilot in the high Gz state.

Blood flow across the body is a combination of muscles and blood pressure. Blood naturally wants to pool in the legs as part of gravity, but pressure and a constant flow makes it easy to keep blood flowing to the brain. A non-amputated human in a high Gz state has the blood sinking into the legs, since the extra g forces overwhelms the careful balance.

This also happens to amputated people, but the lack of legs means that the blood is pooling closer to the heart, meaning the pressure differential at the heart is less. This leads to a higher likelihood that the increased blood pressure near the heart will push blood upward into the brain.

When you get a copyright strike on YouTube, you get a name and an email. No indication of what infringed on the copyright or who the person really is -- it's a dangerous system if abused. Despite reaching out to the email address immediately, I have yet to receive a response. I've reached out again and hope to hear back. That said, I will figure out a way to get the video out to you this afternoon, even if it means having to just divide the episode into two more parts and uploading both at the same time (ugh!).

Watching in 2023 and looking back post repentance and how huge fnaf has gotten, I really appreciate how reasonable Isaac’s story still is. We’ve gotten tons of elaboration, but the story stays the same at heart. The delirium ending shows a kind of purgatory space and the beast ending gives a more vague heaven sort of thing. (To me, I interpret that as him ascending to whatever ideal afterlife their is after reconciling his religious guilt, I.E. dogma and the beast.) Either way, the mother ending and ascension sequence mainly serve to flesh out isaac’s story, and strengthen the emotional core, making the beast ending specifically really emotional. Compared to the fnaf story, it’s branched out and expanded so much to the point that there’s not much emotion left, if any at all. It’s mainly just answering questions for it’s own sake, at least in my opinion.

I would invite you to revisit this theory. As an Isaac player, this theory can go so much deeper with the items and the bosses. For example: Why is it that when Isaac uses Mom's Bra, enemies freeze? Could it be that Isaac's dad would run out of the bathroom if he saw a pad in the trash? Why is it that Kidney Stone gives you a burst of tears randomly? Why does the vanity give you pills? Why does Mom's Coin Purse give you pills? Why is it that kids make fun of him during the cutscenes for doing what he thinks is normal--better yet, why does Isaac think that his acts in the cutscene are normal? The theory I really wanna see for this game is about Kaz. There's a notable scene where he removes his sunglasses to reveal that his eyes appear milky, as if he's blind. When you first rescue him, you can see very briefly at certain moments that, although Snake asks "did they do something to your eyes" and he replies "no, it's just bright," his eyes actually appear normal. I believe his eye color is actually something like hazel if my memory is correct. Now whether this was an intentional thing or not, he does have normal eyes in that scene. Yet he has milky eyes in the only other scene with his sunglasses off, and in many other scenes you can tell his eyes also have this milky appearance to them when you look closely at his sunglasses in scenes that are somewhat close to his face. I became aware that his eyes seemed weird long before he took his sunglasses off because of this. Despite the fact that the guy looks like he should be entirely blind, he acts as though he can see perfectly fine, other than a brief moment when Quiet retrieves Shabani's necklace and he kinda nudges the necklace around with his cane thing until Ocelot picks it up. And then he goes right back to acting as though he has perfect vision again. He also acts like he's reluctant to open his eyes after removing his sunglasses the one time, indicating that he may be somewhat photosensitive (something that would explain why he always wears the sunglasses, and could explain his reaction/response to Snake when rescued as well as why he wears sunglasses all the time in other games). I have heard everything from cataracts caused by a disease his mother may have had (I believe it was specifically an STD), to somehow he was exposed to some sort of radioactive chemical that may have splashed in his face and blinded him (a la Daredevil) and gave him some sort of radar vision thing where he can "see" but not in the traditional sense. Kaz does make a particular comment in his speech to the Diamond Dogs that "[They] will be [his] eyes." He also seems to sense Quiet when no one else does while she's invisible, but only the one time when she's beside the helicopter. When she first arrives and goes invisible to prove that she could hurt the soldiers on Mother Base but chooses not to take advantage of the surprise that being invisible would grant her, Kaz just kinda follows the soldiers after they locate her with thermal scopes, rather than being like "she's right there you idiots." So I suspect it was maybe intuition or possibly a lack of breeze from that side when the helicopter blades are spinning over them.

My challenge to Game Theory is to come up with an answer to that mystery. I never could figure out how Kaz could interact with other characters even though he appears to be completely blind and even acts as though he is in brief moments. I would like to hear if there's any scientific explanation for this. Granted much of Metal Gear 5 seems to be stuff meant to make people go "how is that possible for 1980" (as was mine and my family's constant question when I played the game), I'm curious what you guys think could be the reason for Kaz's strange ability to see but maybe not see at all.

This theory is really well done and thought through. In fact, ever since ultimate was announced, me and my brother came with our own theory about the game. We still believe this is still the story of Masahiro Sakurai, but we made this a lot darker and sadder. I’ll start with melee, the sequel of Smash 64. This introduces crazy hand, the crazy master hand. His trophy says that he was the hallow feeling of destroying one’s own creation. This was Sakurai’s first point of what he was getting into, he wanted to end the series at melee, but the fans wanted him back, pulling him from the darkness to keep making their games, crazy hand is the embodiment of that. Brawl is next, and Subspace Emissary was AWSOME, but the story still continues. (Spoiler alert for those who haven’t played brawl’s Subspace.) At the near end of the game you meet Tabuu, a force controlling master hand like a puppet, tricking Ganondorf to do the wrong order. Ganondorf attacks, but is easily defeated, Master hand try’s to fight as well, but also beats him easily. While Game Theory’s point of Tabuu does make sense, I think it represents us, the players. The ones who keep Sakurai to keep adding what they want. We are controlling the creator like a puppet to keep adding more things for them, to make it more competitive. Sakurai made this game for fun, but all games have a competitive side to them, melee was a super competitive game, but still could be played be new players. Anyway back to Subspace, after beating the Great Maze, Tabuu tries to end all the characters again, but this time, forever. But at the last moment, Sonic swoops in and saves them all. Sonic represents those who support Sakurai, those helping him to keep going and make games. Then you defeat Tabuu, which is insanely hard to do sometimes, but after defeating him, or in this case, the players who keep asking for more, this is the players realizing (kinda) that they can’t ask for too much from Sakurai, and they will mostly respect what he does now. Smash 4 unfortunately does not have a story mode, but does introduce Master Core. Master Core, like Game Theory said, breaks out of Master Hand, this is Master hand losing his mind, and now can’t take anymore. While Crazy Hand escapes, Master Core, or the feelings of Sakurai, break out. Master Cores first mode is a giant person, and yes, each mode represents something. Mode one has a lot of moves that push the player away, this is Sakurai telling the player to go away, to leave him alone. Mode two is a scorpion, this mode is super offensive and likes to attack a lot. This is Sakurai now fighting the player to leave him be and stop bringing him back. Mode three is Sword mode, which has a lot of multi hit attacks one big swing move, and a five hit move. This one is Sakurai saying all the things he has done (multi hit moves) the main point of the game (The big swing) and the things he gets in return (The five hit move). Mode 4 is a copy mode, this is still Master Hands creativity still in Master Core. This is Sakurai saying that these are the characters he has created and that the sequals, which are meant to be better the the previous installments, are his hope that people will get off he’s back for making more Smash. Mode 5 (If your difficulty is high enough) is Master Fortress, a last line of defense to defend the ball. This is you getting into Sakurai’s head, this is his last line of defense against you, and each time you hit the Ball, your hitting points in his head, your saying, “I want this, I want this, I want this.” If you somehow manage to beat Master Fortress, you now hit his Core, the core that does nothing unless out don’t beat it in a certain amount of time. The music is dead, the timer has stopped, you can’t hear anything except your character beating the Core. This is Sakurai giving up, telling you that you win in the end, he can’t take it anymore and now he knows that what he wants to create isn’t what the fans want. Ultimate is him giving what the fans want, everyone is back, fan favorites are here, all just for you. He still has the bit of the game he wanted, but this new smash bros his him giving up and handing over what the fans want. This is my theory, and this is how I think Smash’s story goes. So the next time you fight Master hand and Master Core, think about what you’ve done, or not done, to Sakurai. The people that asked for more out of Sakurai, this is what you’ve done to Sakurai, the smash God. But Remember, that’s just a Theory, a Fan Theory. Thanks for reading.

I think another big reason this is happening is just over saturation. Remember youtube 3-4 years ago? There was just not that much stuff. For example, in the EDU/STEM scene of youtube, where our channel belongs – a few years ago there were only a few "big" channels you had to watch: minutephysics, cgpgrey, crash course, scishow, veritasium, Vsauce. That was not that much and for example crash course and scishow had a much smaller output than today.
Nowadays there are SO many "new" channels in that field that produce great videos. Like the brainscoop, itsoktobesmart, an army of PBS channels, Scishow space, healthcare triage and loads of small channels (like for example "thisplace") that do really interesting things. I remember the time when I watched every new video with edu/science content, of all the good channels in this field on youtube. Nowadays it is impossible to keep up and there are channels I watch only a video or two a month or less, although I love them and never am disappointed.

It is not likely that this will get better in the future. Big channels with millions of monthly views and millions of subscribers still will do ok. It is easier to get deals and the adds still pay not super bad on that level.

But it forces medium sized channels to look for other ways of funding or they just can’t really exist. Like the PBS Channels. They NEVER could exist without their funding from a larger entity. The views just don’t cut it, not even close.
This is not totally a bad thing, you have to get creative. We do work for hire on the side and manage ok. But, like the video said, one chance in algorithm could smash our views and force us to abandon youtube and our channel. Which would be horrible.

So yeah. Hopefully that doesn’t happen.

Matt. You're a genius. You've literally gotten the maximum possible likes with the minimal effort possible. You've subconsciously *ordered* us to like the video. This entire video is a huge likebait and viewbait for the entire channel. Considering how much you talk about subliminal messages and how they're everywhere, it's a bit queer how you've employed them so well here.

At 2:27 you set into out minds that liking and subscribing is an option (showing the word, talking about it). Now, of course, little to nobody is going to do this on command. It's not that easy. However, this reminds us about a like button even existing, placing the image in out subconscious, (some of us even did it at that point that would rather have not, with forgetting about it in the first place), and might make some people think "Well, i like the video so far, might as well do it after". This sets up the possibility of a like at the end, and a sure like afterwards for most people, simply because you drill it in so hard later on.

2:59 - You show a liked "like' button, while also showing that viewing the video helps the creator live their life. I guarantee you, if the subliminal "Like to keep me alive" hasn't come across someone's mind, I'll eat my hat. This plays to our morality. "Well, liking this video will help Matt create more! And will let me see more, as a result. Also, it'll keep him alive and happy with minimal effort on my part! Why not?"

Around 8:10, you show the like count on another video. Because many people either like your channel more than they like that other one, they'll want your video to have more likes because they believe (for whatever reasoning) that they want you to be superior, via more likes to show dominance. It's a territorial thing we have embedded in our minds, and your channel is the figurative "turf" (weird, huh?)

This is possibly the most effective use of your method.

6:29 - 6:39 - "If you click on every game theory video, it'll show up in your feed, bonus points if you like and comment" This is possibly the most dastardly thing you could do. No sublimity, pure words. That sentence coerces us into "Liking" any one of your videos, to be able to see more of your work. Now, as most people don't want to go to some random video that they have every possibility to hate and want to get over liking ASAP, they'll like this one for convenience. This could supply an indefinite number of likes, based on whoever could stumble on your videos and want to see more of you. That sentence alone guaranteed you an unnamed number of likes.

This is wrong how at every single moment that you could, you put into our heads that we should like your videos.

2 things I'd like to bring up for the validity of Link being able to use the Long Shot from Ocarina of Time

1)  Link has super human strength, being able to push an over 9 ton block of stone.  For instance, the stone blocks in the Fire Temple are approximately double the size of Link.  with a cubic meter of generic stone weighing in at a whopping 2,515kg, we determine that the block would weigh around 8551kg, which is over 18,800lbs.  Being able to exert that much force requires tremendous strain on muscles, ligaments, and tendons, yet Link is able to move them with a few grunts, without the use of the Silver or Gold Gauntlets

2) What if the material of the Long Shot was made by a different metal than a steel alloy?  Scandium and Beryllium are similar to steal with hardness and tinsel strength, but are much less dense.  If we assumed the Long Shot was made with Scandium, the tool would weigh about 64lbs.  If it was made out of Beryllium, it would weigh approximately 40lbs.  With these weights, it would be more in the realm of possibility for the Long Shot to be able to function without permanently damaging the user

Ok, but bear with me for a second (pun intended, it’ll make sense soon, I hope)
If one considers that Hyrule is a place that exists/existed/will existo n Earth, then one should also assume that each day/night cycle should last 24 hours, right?
However, according to Zelda’s Wiki, each day on Ocarina of Time (OoT) lasts ~2,5 Real Life minutes (I’ll call them RL, for short), and each night lasts ~1,3 RL minutes. So, we could say that each OoT Hour during the Day lasts something around 12 RL Seconds, and each OoT Hour during the Night lasts about 6 RL Seconds
In that case, after some magical rule of three math, one could conclude that ONE RL Second represents 300 OoT DAY Seconds and 600 OoT NIGHT Seconds.
Now things start to get weird/interesting.
Let’s talk about Day Time only, for now. The Longshot travels roughly at 20m/RL Second, which we now know represents around 300 OoT Seconds. Being so, the Longshot is, in fact, traveling 20 Meters in 300 OoT Seconds, not in 1 Second – in one OoT second, it travels only 0,03 Meters and thus its acceleration equals 0,03 m/(s^2). Throwing all of this in F = m X a, we now have F = 86kg (already brilliantly calculated by The Game Theorists) X 0,03 m/(s^2): Longshot’s Force applied over Link while it’s being fired is only around 2,58 Newtons during the day (even less during the night: 1,29 N). 
I’m pretty sure I’m ignoring a lot of important things here, but still, moving on.
With all that said, one could finally infer a few things:
1) Link could, theoretically, fire the Longshot (and be pulled by it) without having his bones and internal organs crushed
2) Link is, in fact, an EXTREMELY slow hero and the whole game had to be accelerated so that we wouldn’t die before being able to finish it
3) Link's so clumsy that he goes even slower at night so that he won't accidently trip on something while running.
4) I believe that if one would also calculate the actual force applied by Link when he swings his sword, one would also find out that, actually, every enemy in Hyrule is really really weak/breakable and/or that Link’s weapons are actually made of some crazy powerful stuff
5) All of this without even mentioning that there are some places in Hyrule where time stops, and that's creepy and I won't test my really weak math skills in that territory

Welcome, to my game theory! What you said about Call of Duty: Modern Warfare is wrong. What you see in the game isn't regeneration, it's something else. The blood on the screen represents what happens in the battlefield. When a soldier gets hit by a bullet or is injured, but the damage is minimal, and not fatal.
