Hey Theorist Crew, in light of the new Five Nights at Freddy's game and the facts it has, I don't think your nightmare theory would work anymore. I thought that it could be altered to fit a theory where Mike Schmidt could have been the bite victim now left in his own personal hell and the suit be a representation of what he used to lure the kids in. But after looking further into I don't think that works either.

From what I gathered the new game takes place during "the bite of 87" that's referenced in the first game as evidenced by the check you get stating that it is 11-12-1987. The pay on the check also fits minimum wage for that time period as well (3.35ph). But the piece that broke your theory is the name on the check being Jeremy Fitzgerald (has anyone else noticed that both names belong to two prominent baseball players?-haven't looked into them yet). This person is completely different but, the man who completed a week before you went to day shift prior to the start of the game. I thought he could be the Mike from the first one, but I don't think it makes sense now because of a discrepancy in the dates that perplexes me. One of the newspaper clippings from the first game states that the first incident with two children being lured had been solved by the cameras on the night of June 26th and the culprit had been caught the next morning with the children missing. That is roughly five months before the 1987 incident takes place. This could be from the "Fredbear's Family Diner" place referenced by Phone Guy on night six of the second game explaining the bad reputation he talks about in the first night. However, the clipping from the first game specifically states that the incident happened in a "pizzeria" which is what this restaurant just reopened as. This could just be something the author forgot about or maybe this whole thing was just made up to mess with his fans or a whole list of things. But I can't seem to let go of the day shift man's involvement with this. In night six Phone guy also references someone taking a spare "yellow"suit and "they" who are not acting right. This could be the Golden Freddy reference we've been looking for. The timing would have been right and would explain why he complained about the animatronics following him at night. The 2.0 versions have been outfitted with face recognition tech that's been connected to a criminal database. This would explain their protective behavior towards children leading them to attack anyone who threatens them i.e. they bit the person who was kidnapping the children (they were only doing their job). I think this is also alluded to and foreshadowed by Phone Guy who mentions on night four that the place is under investigation and the animatronics act strange around adult humans, but not children. Then there's also night three where Phone Guy mentions "horrible rumors". So I think the kidnapping was going on throughout the week until day five (this is ignoring the June date of course) when the place us put on lock down and Phone Guy (yet again) mentions that a day shift position just opened (and this could be that either he was arrested or he was bitten and killed). Then the link that leads to some of the story in the first game is that on night six Phone guy tells you to take day shift and to keep an eye on the animatronics to make sure they don't "hurt" anyone. He also mentions that he'll be taking night shift which explains why he was there to get caught in the first game.

Then there's the "OG" animatronics that I think are clearly from the diner. They're old and broken down making it easy to believe that they're first gen. And Phone Guy even mentions that they were outfitted with some of the new tech, but were scrapped because they were "too ugly looking". This plays into the first game. The 2.0 versions were most likely scrapped because of the bit incident leaving only the older versions, which by looking at them in the first game were most likely revamped and completely upgraded. I think the fact that the light flicking trick to put them into "reset mode" (i think) not working in the first game fits, because the gen 1's and 2's both were susceptible to that. This furthers my upgraded gen 1 theory. And the mucus and blood coming from them could be from the missing children who were probable stuffed inside because they were the only suits not in use at the time. I also think this can be used to demonstrate that the company was going through a hard financial time given all the lawsuits they would have had to deal with.

There's also something about that marionette in the prize room. Phone Guy expresses his dislike of it say that "it's always thinking and can go anywhere". The fact that he says it can think peaks my interest alone. Not one of the other animatronics are described in that way. There is something special about it and it does act much like the original Foxy in that it can run strait to the player, but it's held back by music. Thing that got me most was the mini-games that happen after certain characters catch you (mainly the older versions and I don't know all the requirement or sequences in which they happen). There is one that has you as a Freddy character (could be golden or regular) where you start in a room with a computer. You venture out to find what looks like the marionette over a puddle of blood and proceed to follow him to a room with a giant present and what looks like a lifeless body next to it. You can also start out in different rooms, one of which has  what looks like the other deactivated animatronics in it. The're one where you have to feed six children cake as Freddy again, but there's a child that's standing outside the building who appears to be crying. You can't really go to him so you keep feeding the kids as a car approaches the child outside and your character slows down. When an adult figure steps out your character stops completely and the child stops crying as his eyes turn into black squares and his body starts distorting. As the adult figure drives away the child turns into a grey figure that either resembles a naked endoskeleton (like the one that can be found in the prize room where the marionette is at 3am on the sixth night and has been said to fit the outline of the Freddy character and may be linked to the Golden Freddy) or the marionette which jumps out at you before the game ends. There's also one that has you play as the old Foxy who has to race to a room with five children in it. Upon reaching the children fireworks go off and a congrats message. It has you do that three times, but on the third time there is a tall purple figure in the lower left corner of the room where you start. In the next room the five children are replaced with eyeless gray figures much like the altered child you see towards the end of the cake game, but this time the old Foxy jumps at you. This might have been telling a part of the story where the animatronics were trying to save the children and would reinforce my theory about the protective nature the animatronics may have exhibited with children. The one that catches my attention the most is the one where the marionette-like figure from the giant present mini-game  appears in a room with four lifeless bodies appear in each corner. The game tells you to "give presents" and you go to each of them and leave a present in front of them. But then it tells you to "give life" and you go to each of them and leave a head of one of the four main animatronics on each corpse and then a broken down Golden Freddy head jumps out at you. Maybe the Marionette has something to do with the possessions of the animatronics in the first game. I noticed that none of the main animatronics really make any vocal noises in the game (from what I've seen on YouTube playthoughs so far). But in the first game you hear the raspy sounds coming form Chica and Bonnie. Then there's the child's laugh that Freddy has. So I that that marionette has a lot to do with the story and how the first game came to be. I can understand the reference to the gifts given his location in the game being in the prize room. And perhaps its gift to the children who's lives were ended prematurely was further existence on this earth in what might have been the only way he new how to "reanimate" them. Or it could be that the corpses inside the the suits could not escape them, being stuck in there for may years. Plus this would also play into the protective nature over children I mentioned earlier. And on a "side" note I've noticed that no one of the forums I've seen so far mentioned that the audio in the mini-games appear to be spelling something different in each mini-game. Some letters are hard to make out thought because the audio's kind of distorted (almost like that Robosapien toy my younger brothers used to be crazy about when it was the new hot toy on the block). I pegged the life one as H-E-O-E-T(or P)-H-E-O-H-E-O-E-T(or P)-H-E-O-H-E-O-E before the Golden Freddy pops up. I'm still not sure what these letters could mean or spell though. I also think these mini-games are illustrating pieces of the story not told in the normal game mode in fragmented and obscure segments.

There are plenty of theories out there as you know, but this is what I've gathered so far. I though you might be interested in doing a followup episode in light of the new game release and I'd be very interested to see what you can do with this. Oh, I also left another episode idea comment for an interpretation on dream village in Animal Crossing: New Leaf called Aika Village on the Five Nights at Freddy's video about a week ago if you want to check it out. It's a village set up in a linear way to tell a story about a girl and her "red dolly" that incorporates some religious and Japanese cultural (Gaijin Boombah cough cough) icons along with some very stylized and well placed imagery. There are many different interpretations of the story and it's outcome and I though it would be something you guys might have fun researching. Either way I really enjoy your work and can't wait for the next video. I wish you all well. Cheers.

This is a video I have to comment on before I actually watch it, because it's a subject that's come up before in my circles and it's really a lot simpler than people make it. People usually approach health stats as literally representing health, and damage as wounds. At full HP you have no wounds, and at 0 you would presumably have suffered damage to literally 100% of your body tissue, even though you should have died long, long before that point.

The thing is that in all games of all genres, all stats, including health, are abstractions, and all your defensive stats, like health, armor, dodge chance, etcetera, represent the ability to avoid injury. Dying at 0 health is pretty much just a time saver; you would otherwise be incapacitated until you died of some other cause, assuming you weren't reduced to 0 by being blown apart or hit with a precision kill like a headshot. Regenerating health, therefore, is just catching your breath and letting your brain catch up, coping with the superficial wounds you've sustained thus far, and preparing yourself to go back into the fight. People just never seem to be able to understand the purpose of abstractions in gaming, even though gaming itself pretty much consists entirely of abstractions.

I listet up every category MatPat uses and which Links are mentioned there.
I don't know the 2D games so well, besides A Link to the Past and Oracle of Seasons, so please keep that in mind. I did research on Zeldawiki when I was in doubt though.
I tried to rank the Links by points ranging from 0 to 3. The winner gets up to 3 points, follow-ups who also stand out get 2 or 1 point(s), while every not-outstanding Link gets 0 points.
If there are more Links than 3 in a category, I included decimal numbers (by x.5). Not entirely sure about my mathematical distribution, but I think it works in general.

As a result they place less value on story and more value on graphics cooperative play and competitive play, areas in which Nintendo systems and games have fallen behind their competitors.

The innovations there were not bolt on options or rushes to the marketplace, but purposeful design choices. Something was touched on in this video, but was not quite followed through on. It mentioned that the reason games like Call of Duty and Madden sell so well is because they appeal to a wider demographic -- a demographic of "non-gamers".

That is, people who aren't normally into video games as a rule also buy them. People who aren't normally into video game wouldn't buy something like Portal, typically. So obviously it appeals mostly to the gaming community, a smaller demographic, and doesn't sell as well. Even something like Mario Party 8 is very appealing to people who don't play games, and especially to children.

Even flappy bird was mentioned at the end, and I think it's safe to say a lot of the people playing flappy bird have little interest in gaming.

It would be interested in seeing what the stats are for the gaming habits of people who play games like Call of Duty, as well as the stats on the buying habits of people who also purchase games like Portal. What it boils down to is: who is buying which games and why? Of all of the figures in this video, that was the one thing that wasn't looked into.

I don't think the gaming community doesn't want innovation. I think what this comes down to is that games are now appealing to a wider base of people rather than just a community of people who take an interest in games, and those games that appeal to that wider base will obviously sell better.
So in a nutshell, gamers are nostalgia-blinded.

When I first watched this video, I couldn't help but think the Wii U was no different than the Virtual Boy, but now I don't believe that's necessarily the case--let me explain why:

1. Batteries: Nintendo has released higher capacity batteries for Wii U controllers able last up to 8 hours. Buying them individually may cost you around $30, but that price will surely go down over time. A wired connection is always an option though if you don't want to pay the extra price...

2. Expensive Technology: Not really. The gamepad is the biggest problem, sure, but the Wii U is still at least $100 cheaper than the PS4. Also, we have yet to see if Nintendo will make that gap even larger via a price cut or controller switch (from gamepad to pro controller).

3. Rushed Technology: Yes there was a rush, but it was minimal in comparison to the 360, which, despite the millions of faulty red-ring systems released, still managed to hold its ground. 

4. Games: Nintendo may have been ultra-slow at releasing quality titles for the Wii U over the past year-and-a-half, but now it seems things are ramping up. 

For instance, there's Mario Kart 8 and Smash Bros. 4 (both of which are successful sequels), the eShop retro game releases, Bayonetta 2 exclusively for Wii U (another sequel), Hyrule Warriors (should have "Zelda" in name), the Xeno rpg (once again, another sequel), and some promising multiconsole titles, such as Watchdogs and LEGO The Hobbit.

Mario and Smash probably won't help the console recover exclusively, but collectively, with all other games listed above, there is potential to see such a thing happen.

And let's not forget E3--Nintendo may still have a few tricks left (they are Nintendo, after all)


In the end, nothing is truly certain, but if Nintendo properly connects advertisement and promotion with a cheaper price tag, a better, expansive game library, more third-party support, and a controller redesign/transition (including longer battery life), they will have a much higher probability of making it back into the competition with only a few bumps and bruises left over.

So in other words, if you owned a Wii prior to the Wii U's release, additional costs were NON EXISTENT. Lastly, neither WiiMotes, nor games are REQUIRED for the Wii U to function. Lastly, the Price cut in August 2013 pretty much eliminated this issue permanently.

3. Although i will admit that the Wii U was rushed, that was merely to get an edge on Nintendo's competitors, Sony and Microsoft. As for the supposed "sacrificed graphics", i don't think you know what HD means, as the Wii U is clearly an HD console, unless you think that HD = Photo-realism, which is false, as further proof, the latest games for the Wii U can run games at a NATIVE 1920x1080p at 60 fps, crappy graphics my ass.

4. The games- Yes, the Wii U's launch line up wasn't perfect, but its library is growing more and more, and with big name titles like Mario Kart 8 and Smash Bros Wii U, both of which are a part of franchises that are known to be console sellers. You've also got games like Mario Party 10, Super Mario 3D World, and hell even Wii Sports Club. As far as i'm concerned, the Wii U's Game Library is strong, and getting stronger with more 3rd party support titles like bayonetta 2. Don't even start about the Gamepad, i've seen it used in some pretty unique ways as of late, so there goes that point. Some examples being its use as a controller for Mario Kart 8 (motion based) and Smash Bros for Wii U (non-motion based), as well as its uses in Wii Sports Club for things like pitching in baseball and teeing off in golf. Hell, the best example of the gamepad being used correctly is Game & Wario, where the ENTIRE GAME is BUILT around the gamepad. So, although i admit it was a bit gimmicky to start out with, the gamepad is FAR from a gimmick now. Lastly, there are 457 Games in the Wii U Library (this counts both disc and digital, including eShop stuff and Virtual Console.)

5. Third party support- Sorry MatPat, your argument fails here considering that the Wii U HAS third party support, and has been gaining more. The four companies you have as an example likely ALL have games on the Wii U. (with the exception of Zynga, but they don't count because they do mobile games for iOS and Android devices.) Ubisoft has Rayman Legends among other Ubi titles to make it to Wii U, Popcap is a part of EA, who themselves have a great number of games on Wii U. Lastly, Third party devs did NOT flee from the Wii U, they were simply cautious about it and didn't want to produce games for Wii U right away.

6. Final notes. The Wii U might've struggled a bit first, but has since geared up and looks to have a more successful life down the road. With 457 Games in the library (third party titles included), fairer pricing, bundles, Wii Backwards compatibility, and HD 1080p Graphics, i can officially say that the Wii U is NOT the "new VirtualBoy".

I've been digging into this "why do people play" topic lately, and I'm not sure I agree with the popular understanding.
From what I can tell the primary cornerstone is "purpose".

This comes largely from self-application. Applying yourself to a problem or challenge gives you a sense of purpose if that problem is meaningful to you. 
This covers "competence" and "autonomy" pretty well.

Purpose can also come from narrative, setting, how much your actions impact the situation, overall comprehension of your role, etc.

Outside of purpose, the reasons we play can be boiled down to more sentimental experiences such as novelty or nostalgia.
